title: Purposes and results: in order to, so as to, etc.
subtitle: so as to reduce noise / so that she could finish
summary: Express purpose with in order / so as + to-infinitive and with in order that / so that, and introduce results with such that and in such a way that / as to.

lesson.heading: in order to and so as to
lesson.text: To talk about the purpose of an action we can use **in order** or **so as** + to-infinitive. In spoken English in particular it is much more common simply to use a to-infinitive on its own with the same meaning.

examples.text: He took the course **in order to** get a better job.
Trees are being planted by the roadside **so as to** reduce traffic noise.
He took the course **to** get a better job.
examples.note: the everyday version - no in order / so as

lesson.heading: Negative purpose: so as not to / in order not to
lesson.text: We rarely use just *not* + to-infinitive. Instead we use **so as not to** or **in order not to**.

examples.text: He kept the speech vague **in order not to** commit himself to one side or the other.
I wrote down her name **so as not to** forget it.
examples.wrong: her name not to forget it

lesson.note: In contrastive sentences not + to-infinitive is fine: I came to see you not (in order / so as) to complain, but (in order / so as) to apologise.

lesson.heading: to-infinitive or a clause?

left.label: in order / so as + to-infinitive
examples: She stayed at work late **in order to** complete the report.
She stayed at work late **so as to** complete the report.

right.label: in order that / so that + clause
examples: She stayed at work late **in order that** she could complete the report.
She stayed at work late **so that** she could complete the report.

lesson.note: Never in order that / so that + to-infinitive. So that is more common than in order that and less formal; informally we can drop that after so, but we always keep it after in order.

lesson.heading: Tenses after in order that / so that
lesson.text: A present tense verb in the main clause is usually followed by a present tense verb, or a modal with present or future reference (can, will). A past tense verb is usually followed by a past tense verb or a modal with past reference (could, would). Modals are very common here.

examples.text: Regular checks are made **in order that** safety standards **are maintained**.
Advice is given **in order that** students **can** choose the best course.
Did you give up your job **so that** you **could** take care of your mother?
I hid the presents **so that** Marianna **wouldn't** find them.

lesson.heading: such that (formal)
lesson.text: In formal contexts, such as academic writing, we can use **such that** to introduce a result. It means 'in a way that has the result that ...'.

examples.text: The model was designed **such that** the value of x could be calculated.

lesson.heading: in such a way that / as to
lesson.text: Less formally we can use **in such a way that** + clause, or **in such a way as** + to-infinitive, with a similar meaning.

examples.text: The advertisement is printed **in such a way that** two very different pictures can be seen depending on how you look at it.
Our business is managed **in such a way as to** minimise its environmental impact.

lesson.heading: such + noun phrase + that
lesson.text: We can also introduce a result with **such** + noun phrase + **that**.

examples.text: It is **such** a popular play **that** all the performances were sold out after the first day.

lesson.text: If the purpose clause has its own subject, you need in order that / so that; if the subject is the same as in the main clause, a to-infinitive is usually enough.

exercises.prompt: Bus fares in the city were being cut ___ encourage people to use public transport.
exercises.explanation: A positive purpose takes in order to or so as to.

exercises.prompt: We crept quietly towards the deer ___ frighten them away.
exercises.explanation: For a negative purpose we use so as not to or in order not to, not plain 'not to'.

exercises.prompt: Match each action with the purpose behind it.

pairs.left: He packed his suitcase with the books at the bottom
pairs.right: so as not to crush his clothes.
in order to prevent people walking across the grass.

pairs.left: I walked around the outside of the field
pairs.right: so as not to damage the growing crops.

pairs.left: She looked down at the book in front of her
pairs.right: in order to avoid his gaze.

pairs.left: The roadworks were carried out at night
pairs.right: so as not to disrupt traffic too much.

pairs.left: I had to borrow money from the bank
pairs.right: in order to set up the business.

exercises.prompt: She stayed at work late in order that she ___ the report.
exercises.explanation: In order that is followed by a clause, very often with a modal - never by a to-infinitive.

exercises.prompt: I put a rug over the stain on the carpet so that nobody ___ it was there.
exercises.explanation: A past tense in the main clause (put) is followed by a modal with past reference.

exercises.prompt: There were screens on all the windows so that mosquitoes ___ in.
exercises.explanation: There were is past, so the so that clause takes could, not can.

exercises.prompt: The software is designed so that it ___ up a lot of computer memory.
exercises.explanation: A present tense in the main clause (is designed) is followed by a modal with present or future reference.

exercises.statement: He kept the speech vague not to commit himself to one side or the other.
exercises.explanation: He kept the speech vague in order not to / so as not to commit himself to one side or the other. Plain 'not to' is not used for a negative purpose here.

exercises.statement: It is such a popular play that all the performances were sold out after the first day.
exercises.explanation: Correct. such + noun phrase + that introduces a result.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite 'The website is organised such that it is easy to navigate' less formally.
exercises.answer: The website is organised in such a way that it is easy to navigate.
exercises.explanation: in such a way that is the less formal equivalent of the academic such that.

exercises.prompt: The meeting room is designed in such a way ___ allow everyone's voice to be heard without microphones.
exercises.explanation: Before a to-infinitive the pattern is in such a way as to; before a clause it is in such a way that.

exercises.prompt: Can the purpose be expressed with a plain to-infinitive (no in order / so as), or does it need so as / in order?
categories: Needs so as not to / in order not to

items.text: I had to borrow money from the bank to set up the business.
Bus fares were cut to encourage people to use public transport.
She looked down at the book to avoid his gaze.
We put up a fence to prevent people walking across the grass.
He packed the books at the bottom not to crush his clothes.
I walked around the field not to damage the growing crops.
We crept towards the deer not to frighten them away.
